title: Demand for EV chargers is outstripping supply, says ChargePoint report
gist: ChargePoint data shows 2025 charging sessions rose 34 percent while new charger installations grew only 16 percent, opening a structural supply gap that CEO Rick Wilmer frames around a 30 percent workplace-utilization threshold beyond which drivers cannot find an open charger. Wilmer argues the North American EV market is healthier than press coverage implies — 1.8 million EVs sold through August, 96 percent EV retention rates, rising used-EV prices, and escalating fuel prices pulling in previously skeptical buyers.

insights.claim: ChargePoint's 2025 data shows charging sessions grew 34 percent while new charger installations grew only 16 percent, a roughly two-to-one demand-over-supply gap in EV charging infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Utilization per installed charger is rising fast, which improves unit economics for existing charging assets and supports a hardware replacement and expansion cycle.
insights.quote: for 2025, its data shows that there was a 34 percent increase in charging sessions, yet new charger installations only grew by 16 percent

insights.claim: ChargePoint CEO Rick Wilmer says 30 percent utilization is the breaking point for workplace charging on a five-day, eight-hour-per-day pattern — above that, drivers routinely arrive and cannot find an open charger.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: A concrete 30 percent utilization ceiling is a sizing rule for modeling how many chargers a given EV fleet actually requires — far more than naive utilization math implies.
insights.quote: on a five-day, eight-hour-a-day workplace scenario, if you’re above 30 percent utilization, you’re going to have drivers coming in that can’t find an open charger
insights.locator: So what we’ve determined, especially for

insights.claim: Workplace charging creates a self-reinforcing demand loop: employees demand chargers, the employer installs a few, other employees then buy EVs because charging exists, and utilization blows past the 30 percent threshold leaving staff angrier than before charging was offered.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Initial workplace charger orders systematically undersize; expect repeat expansion orders from the same accounts, a favorable land-and-expand dynamic for charging vendors.
insights.quote: So they put some in, and then other employees now have charging at work, so they buy EVs, and all of a sudden you’re up above 30 percent.
insights.locator: And it’s fascinating to watch this happen

themes.theme: EV demand is stronger than the narrative

insights.claim: More than 1.8 million EVs were sold between the start of 2026 and the end of August according to analysts, even as general optimism about EV adoption has cooled from a few years ago.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Volume keeps compounding despite sentiment deterioration — a classic sentiment-versus-fundamentals divergence worth fading.
insights.quote: More than 1.8 million EVs had already been sold between the start of this year and the end of August, according to analysts.
insights.locator: There might not be the same degree of optimism

insights.claim: Escalating US fuel prices with no clear end in sight have produced a large uptick in drivers considering EVs they had written off the prior year, making gasoline price levels a direct demand input for charging infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Charging and EV-adjacent names carry an embedded long-oil-price option; watch pump prices as a leading indicator of consideration-set shifts.
insights.quote: there has been a large uptick in drivers considering EVs that they might have written off last year, due to escalating fuel prices with no clear end in sight
insights.locator: There might not be the same degree of optimism

insights.claim: Wilmer cites EV retention rates of 96 percent — drivers coming off leases are moving to another EV rather than back to gas — which means each EV sold is close to a permanent addition to charging demand.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Near-total retention makes the installed EV base a durable annuity for charging networks, supporting long-duration infrastructure capex.
insights.quote: EV retention rates are 96 percent. So those folks that are putting their leased cars on the used market, they’re not going back to gas, they’re going to another EV
insights.locator: All in all, things are moving forward

insights.claim: Wilmer reads rising used-EV prices as evidence of excess demand, arguing appetite is there whenever a vehicle hits the right price point — used EVs at price parity with equivalent gas vehicles are clearing strongly.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Used-EV transaction prices are a cleaner real-time demand gauge than new-vehicle incentives-distorted sales; track them.
insights.quote: When you look at how much interest there is in the used EVs that are at parity with an equivalent gas vehicle, that tells you the appetite is there for EVs if it’s the right vehicle at the right price point
insights.locator: Beyond that, cheap electric trucks from Slate and Ford

insights.claim: Wilmer contends forward-looking EV forecasts fail to account for improving product-market fit as OEMs finally introduce the vehicles North American buyers want, implying consensus adoption forecasts are biased low.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: If product-market fit is the missing variable, the upside surprise comes from cheap electric trucks like Slate's and Ford's rather than from subsidies.
insights.quote: I don’t think a lot of the forward-looking forecasts accommodate the fact that the product market fit is getting better coming out of the car companies
insights.locator: Beyond that, cheap electric trucks from Slate and Ford

insights.claim: ChargePoint's RFP volume for charging solutions has not slowed and the company reported quarter-over-quarter growth in its last reported quarter, which Wilmer uses as evidence that North American charging demand is better shaped than press coverage suggests.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: RFP pipeline is a forward booking indicator; management pointing to it rather than backlog conversion is worth verifying against reported numbers.
insights.quote: Part of it is just the data we see in terms of the amount of RFPs that we receive for charging solutions. They haven’t slowed down.
insights.locator: All in all, things are moving forward

insights.claim: ChargePoint has launched cheaper, more powerful Level 2 AC 240 V chargers for North America and partnered with Eaton's smart breaker technology to enable bidirectional charging at a price point aimed at basic vehicle-to-home backup rather than energy arbitrage.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: The first mass V2H wedge is outage backup, not grid revenue — position around resilience demand and smart-panel suppliers like Eaton rather than V2G market design.
insights.quote: We’re really pushing to get to a point where you can do a vehicle-to-home solution at a much, much lower price point than what’s available today

insights.claim: Wilmer says widespread vehicle-to-grid is blocked because most vehicles on the market are only DC bidirectional, and a DC bidirectional home solution is far too expensive and physically too large — cars must become AC bidirectional first.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: V2G timelines depend on OEM vehicle architecture changes, not charger hardware; discount near-term V2G revenue assumptions in any charging model.
insights.quote: the first thing you need is cars that are AC bidirectional. Most of the vehicles in the market now only are DC bidirectional.
insights.locator: But Wilmer thinks a degree of standardization

insights.claim: Wilmer argues that standardization across both the automotive industry and electrical utilities is a prerequisite to widespread V2G growth, adding a regulatory and interoperability gate on top of the hardware gate.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Two sequential standardization hurdles imply V2G is a multi-year-out option, not a near-term earnings driver for charging companies.
